newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia party parades despite military's warning.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia party parades despite military's warning.

text.p: Supporters of a minority Indonesian party held processions in two major cities on Monday, ignoring warnings by the military that street parades were banned during the general election campaign.
The Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) supporters paraded in the capital Jakarta and in the ancient city of Yogyakarta. They were watched by police, but no attempt was made to stop them.
The military ultimatum came as the PPP, whose party faithful have frequently violated the ruling against street parades, resumed campaigning across Java island on Monday for the May 29 election.

Each of the three parties permitted to contest the election -- the PPP, the ruling Golkar and the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) -- are allotted separate parts of the country in which to campaign each day.

"If they continue to commit violations, then we with great regret will have to take firm action," Jakarta military commander Major-General Sutiyoso was quoted as saying on Sunday by the privately run Media Indonesia newspaper.
Sutiyoso said the military was in a difficult and uncomfortable position because traffic could become congested and public order disturbed if the street parades were allowed to continue.

But more than 10,000 PPP supporters blocked streets in southern Jakarta on Monday as the party held a rally at a sports field. Dressed in the PPP's green colours, they filled trucks and buses and drove in processions with scores of motorcycles.
Many shouted "Hidup (Long Live) PPP", and raced the engines of their vehicles as traffic crawled along at a snail's pace.
In Yogyakarta, PPP supporters held a mock funeral after their procession, which they said symbolised the death of democracy in the country.
The PPP has said it will not campaign in Yogyakarta because of an attack on its party office in the city last week, which it has blamed on supporters of the ruling Golkar party.

The PPP supporters blocked the street heading to Kuncen, one of the party's strongholds in the city, with bamboo sticks and barbed wire. Dozens of soldiers armed with rifles and rubber sticks stood guard.

No violence was reported and the street was reopened soon after the "funeral" ended. Armed soldiers were also seen in several other parts of the city, which is a major tourism centre, and there were occasional patrols by soldiers riding on motorcycles.

Only Golkar flags and banners and those from the other minority party, the PDI, could be seen in Yogyakarta. PPP banners were removed by party officials after the attack on the headquarters. In its place, anti-Golkar posters and graffiti were scrawled on walls in black spray paint.

The three legal parties are vying for the backing of nearly 125 million voters to fill 425 elected seats in the 500-seat House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are alloted to the military, which does not vote.
The Golkar party is seeking to win 70 percent of the vote, up from 68 percent in polls in 1992.
Campaigning for the May 29 poll began on April 27 and ends on May 23.

The ban on street parades was imposed for the first time during this campaign because of fears by authorities that they could spark violence after more than a dozen people were killed in political, religious and ethnic riots on the main island of Java in the past year.
